analysis.one_liner: Extends children's online privacy rules to teens and bans targeted ads aimed at minors.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to protect kids' and teens' online privacy cleared the Senate Commerce Committee and was placed on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have extended the existing children's online privacy law, which covers kids 12 and under, to teenagers as well, so websites and apps could not collect a teen's personal information without clear notice and consent. It would have banned advertising aimed at a specific teen based on that teen's data without the teen's consent, given parents and teens the right to see and delete collected information, and required that internet-connected toys and gadgets sold to children meet federal security standards and explain on the box what data they collect.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers using websites, apps, and connected devices, and their parents, who would gain notice-and-consent rights over data collection, the right to delete collected data, protection from targeted advertising based on a teen's personal information or psychological profiling, and assurance that connected devices marketed to kids meet security standards.

how_it_helps.text: Extends privacy protections that previously applied only to children 12 and under to minors, so a website or app that knows or should know a user is a minor cannot collect personal information without notice and consent [S2] [S3].

Prohibits targeted marketing directed at a child, and at a minor without the minor's consent, ending advertising built on a teen's personal data, psychological profiling, or device tracking [S2] [S4].
Gives parents of children and minors themselves the right to see what personal information was collected, to challenge inaccurate information, and to have it erased or corrected [S2] [S4].

Prohibits the sale of internet-connected devices targeted at children and minors unless they meet federal cybersecurity and data security standards, and requires a plain-language privacy dashboard on the packaging explaining what data the device collects and how it is protected [S2] [S4].
Enforces the rules through the Federal Trade Commission with civil penalties available even for first violations, and lets state attorneys general sue violators on behalf of their residents [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Websites, apps, and connected-device makers that profit from collecting children's and teens' personal data would bear compliance costs: building consent systems, limiting data collection and retention, implementing deletion requests, meeting security standards, and forgoing targeted advertising to minors without consent. Some of those costs could be passed to consumers in prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data-harvesting websites, apps, and device makers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for platforms and device makers would fall partly on consumers and small businesses, and the bill's constructive-knowledge rules would make any operator with data suggesting teens use its service treat all users as minors unless it verifies ages [S4].

Age verification creates its own privacy trade-off: to comply, a service must verify age information for users before collecting anything, meaning platforms would gather age data about everyone, including adults, which the bill's own mixed-audience exemption forces on general-audience sites [S4].
The bill relies heavily on a year of Federal Trade Commission rulemaking before key provisions take effect, so protection would arrive slowly and depend on how the agency writes the rules [S4].

The safe harbor provisions let companies deem themselves compliant by following self-regulatory guidelines drawn up by the marketing and online industries and approved by the FTC, a channel that could blunt the bill's impact [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families, the benefits are concrete and the main costs fall on companies whose business model depends on tracking minors, though some costs reach consumers and the age-verification requirement creates a real, if manageable, privacy tension of its own.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill and it was placed on the Senate's calendar of pending business in December 2022, but the Senate never brought it up for a vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Ed Markey of Massachusetts, author of the original 1998 children's online privacy law, introduced the bill on May 13, 2021, joined by Senators Cassidy, Blumenthal, and Lummis, and it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee [S1] [S4] [S6].
The bill had three cosponsors, two Republicans and one Democrat, giving it support from both parties [S5].
On July 27, 2022, the Senate Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute [S6].

On December 15, 2022, Chair Maria Cantwell reported the bill to the Senate with a substitute amendment, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 658 [S4] [S6].
The bill never received a Senate floor vote, and it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1] [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Social media platforms, app operators, and the online advertising industry are better off, because they continue to collect and monetize children's and teens' personal data without the consent requirements, deletion rights, security standards, or limits on targeted marketing the bill would have imposed. Parents and teens gained nothing, since the existing law still covers only children 12 and under.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from introduction: a Democrat (Markey) and a Republican (Cassidy) led it, joined by a Democrat and a Republican as cosponsors, and the Senate Commerce Committee reported it favorably with a bipartisan membership; no floor vote occurred to show a partisan split.

industries.note: The bill bans targeted marketing directed at a minor without the minor's consent and bars using minors' personal information, psychological profiling, or device identifiers to aim ads, cutting off behavioral advertising aimed at teens. Ads would not simply vanish for minors; they just could not be personalized without consent.

industries.industry: Social media platforms and app operators
industries.note: Platforms would need consent to collect teens' data, honor deletion and correction requests, limit collection and retention, and treat users as minors where data suggests minors use the service, all at real compliance cost to businesses built on data collection.

Device makers selling products to children would have to meet federal cybersecurity and data security standards and print a privacy dashboard on the packaging, a cost of doing business that in exchange gives families verifiable safety information on products marketed to their kids.

The bill lets operators comply by following self-regulatory guidelines drawn up by representatives of the marketing and online industries and approved by the FTC, keeping industry bodies in the gatekeeping role for children's privacy.
